name: Ayuntamiento de Santillana del Mar
skipReason: Administrative building (town hall), not a visitor attraction.
summary: One of the most stately buildings in the town, built in the early 18th century of yellowish sandstone ashlar. From 1833 it was altered to serve as the seat of the town council, and a major interior refurbishment in 1987 adapted it to its administrative role.

name: Capricho de Gaudí
summary: Originally named Villa Quijano, El Capricho is one of the most representative works of Spanish Modernisme. Designed by the Catalan architect Antoni Gaudí and built in 1883–1885, it is one of his very few buildings outside Catalonia. It was commissioned as a summer house by Máximo Díaz de Quijano, a music-loving indiano enriched in Cuba and brother-in-law of the Marquis of Comillas. Music runs through it: iron railings shaped like treble clefs and semiquavers, and tubular window counterweights that chimed like bells. Bands of exposed brick alternate with sunflower-tile friezes, porch capitals show palm leaves and swallows, and the Persian-minaret-style tower blends Arab, Mudéjar and Gothic influences.

name: Casa de Leonor de la Vega
summary: Built at the end of the 15th century and substantially remodelled in the 16th, this house is attributed to Leonor de la Vega, mother of the Marquis of Santillana, Íñigo López de Mendoza. It has been restored and now houses the Hotel Casa del Marqués. The interior is not open to visitors.

name: Casa de los Abades
summary: Probably built at the end of the 17th century, this house originally belonged to the abbots of the Colegiata. Today it is known as the Casa de la Archiduquesa, having been the residence of Archduchess Margarita of Austria-Bourbon. The coats of arms are modern, made by local artist Jesús Otero, and show the emblems of Santillana's most notable lineages (Barreda, Velarde, Cossío, Villa, Bracho, Peredo and others), with the archduchess's arms beside them.

name: Casa de los Hombrones
summary: A Baroque house from the end of the 17th century. It is named after the two soldiers who hold up its coat of arms, whose motto reads "A good death honours a whole life" ("Un buen morir es honra de la vida").

name: Casa de los Quevedo y Cossío
summary: Two late-17th-century houses now joined into one home, with an unusual layout: a tunnel runs through the building as a drain for the drinking trough. The southern house belonged to the Quevedo family, whose coat of arms sits on a parapet of the north front; here you can try the classic glass of milk with sobao or sponge cake. Its curiosity is the door lintel, carved with a mask of Tláloc, the Aztec rain god, common on the doors of indianos' and conquistadors' houses to seek his protection, and featured in María Oruña's novel "Puerto escondido". Attached to the north front is the Cossío house, with one of the town's finest coats of arms.

name: Casas del Águila y la Parra
summary: These two houses stand in the heart of historic Santillana del Mar, on the Plaza Ramón Pelayo (Plaza Mayor), next to the town hall and opposite the Barreda-Bracho house, now the Parador Gil Blas. Fine examples of civil architecture from the 17th and 16th centuries respectively, they belong to the Government of Cantabria and were restored at the end of the 1980s. Between 1988 and 1991 they hosted exhibitions on the ethnography of Cantabria, and since then a number of art exhibitions. Entry is free.

name: Cementerio de Comillas (El Ángel del cementerio)
summary: Lluís Domènech i Montaner designed the remodelling of the cemetery, building the ruins of the old Gothic chapel into its structure and adding a new enclosure wall full of picturesque features (pinnacles, crosses pattée, an entrance arch). His design deliberately heightens the look of a ruin, setting off its outline with the marble Guardian Angel by sculptor Josep Llimona, placed on the walls above the nave of the old church.

name: Centro Cultural El Espolón
summary: In the late 18th century Juan Domingo González de la Reguera, Archbishop of Lima and a native of Comillas, had El Espolón built to house a Chair of Latin Grammar, established by royal decree of King Charles IV in 1789; in 1802 the Real Seminario Cántabro was founded here. Designed by architect Cosme Antonio Bustamante, it was restored in 2009 by Peridis. It now hosts cultural tourism, training, workshops, associations, a library and a telecentre; note its central courtyard and temporary exhibitions. Nearby are the Plaza de la Constitución (old town hall, San Cristóbal church), the Plaza del Corro, the Fuente de los Tres Caños and the Sacred Heart monument.

name: Centro de Recursos, Interpretación y Estudios de la Escuela (CRIEME)
summary: CRIEME is an institution of Cantabria's Education Department for conserving and recovering school heritage. It is based in Polanco, in the house of writer José María de Pereda, who built it in 1872 on the Trascolina meadow because his birthplace was in a poor state. Admired for its modernity, it had three floors, stairs on all four sides, a chapel, a service floor, a laundry and a bathroom. Pereda spent every summer there until 1905. In 1945 the State bought it for the Sección Femenina's school for leaders, which taught there until 1988. After years of decay it was restored in the late 1990s and opened as CRIEME on 28 September 2005.

name: Chalet del Duque de Almodóvar del Río (El Duque)
summary: Designed at the end of the 19th century by Francisco Hernández Rubio for the Prado de San José, this house takes its name from Swiss chalets and its forms from the much-admired English architecture, stressing every typical feature of those supposedly rustic styles: asymmetry, multiple axes, and woodwork and brickwork. It contrasts with the eclecticism of the Palacio de Sobrellano and the Modernisme of Gaudí's Capricho.

name: Colegiata de Santa Juliana
summary: The Colegiata de Santa Juliana grew out of the expansion of the earlier monastery of the same name in the mid-12th century. It was founded by a group of monks to help repopulate the area, with a small hermitage to display the relics of the martyr Juliana that they had brought with them. The village took the monastery's name, "Sancta Iuliana", which evolved into today's Santillana. Its high altarpiece, made between the late 15th and early 16th centuries, blends Flamboyant Gothic and Plateresque elements. Declared a Site of Cultural Interest (BIC) in 1889.

name: Convento de San Ildefonso
summary: Built in 1667 in Baroque style, this convent was richer in income and property than Regina Coeli, and its community often took in young women from the region's leading families and great lineages. After the Dominican nuns left, the Poor Clares, who had lived in the neighbouring convent, took it over. The nuns sell their sweets here.

name: Fachada principal del Cementerio de Comillas
summary: Comillas cemetery has an original Modernista front: a round arch flanked by small paired columns and crowned by a decorated cornice, with a highly ornamental iron gate. A rubble-stone wall topped with decorative pinnacles encloses it, all designed by Domènech. The cemetery reuses the late-Gothic parish church (late 15th–early 16th century), whose ruin is crowned by a marble angel by sculptor Josep Llimona i Bruguera. Some notable mausoleums survive, above all the Piélago family's, designed by Domènech and made by Llimona. It is reached via the approaches to the harbour and beach from the centre of Comillas.

It can be visited free of charge by prior arrangement.

name: Montaña La Masera de Castío
summary: Its north face looked towards the hamlet of Cortiguera, while its south side touched the village of Hinojedo. This singular flat-topped hill rises as a rectangular promontory, solid at its base, an expression of the earth's energy, like a huge, wide stool without a back.

name: Monumento al Marqués de Comillas
summary: Raised by the town of Comillas in memory of Antonio López y López, whose economic and social rise after returning from Cuba and setting up his businesses in Barcelona culminated in 1878, when Alfonso XII made him Marquis of his native Comillas in recognition of his financial and material support against the Cuban insurrection. It stands on a meadow that López's friend Ángel Pérez gave to the town for the monument. Cascante's design, respected by Domènech, has an original ship's-prow pedestal and a column carrying the marquis's statue. Maritime themes abound, and its bronze statues of allegories of the Antilles and the Philippines were especially notable.

name: Mural de Okuda a José María de Pereda
summary: A mural by Okuda on a wall in the La Cochera neighbourhood, at the entrance to the village, featuring the Cantabrian writer José María de Pereda. The work brings together a full set of imagery to portray the Polanco-born author.

name: Museo de Altamira
summary: The museum lies 2 km from the centre of Santillana del Mar. Its history starts with a management board set up in 1924. The first building serving the cave was a traditional mountain house for displaying and conserving finds from the excavations and housing the first guard. Rising visitor numbers led to three pavilions in the 1970s, and in 1979 the Ministry of Culture created the National Museum and Research Centre of Altamira to better manage and conserve the cave. The current building by architect Juan Navarro Baldeweg opened in 2001, its siting and design driven by protecting the cave. It is a state museum of the Ministry of Culture and Sport.
facts: Avenida Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola, Santillana del Mar

name: Museo Diocesano Regina Coeli
summary: Housed in the former Dominican friary of Regina Coeli ("Queen of Heaven"), the museum holds over 800 works from parishes across the region, notable for their popular character and dominated by sculpture, which with stonemasonry was the region's traditional craft. Besides the iconography of popular local saints, it shows Flemish, American and Castilian (mainly Burgos and Valladolid) influences of the Baroque era. Highlights include Gothic sculpture, the San Roque and San Sebastián groups, Hispano-Philippine silks and ivories, enamels and silverwork, especially from America. It also studies and catalogues the Diocese of Santander's heritage and, with the regional government, opens about 50 religious monuments free of charge.

name: Museo Jesús Otero
summary: Sculptor Jesús Otero Oreña left his legacy to his home town in this museum and foundation beside the Colegiata de Santa Juliana. Opened in 1994 with works he donated in 1993, it holds about fifty sculptures, many from his last years, plus the tools, implements and drawings he used. Born in Santillana in 1908, Otero first exhibited in a group show in Santander; a scholarship holder at the San Fernando Academy of Fine Arts, he was strongly influenced by Emiliano Barral and Victorio Macho. Months before his death he donated all his remaining works, and friends and admirers set up the museum in the former Guardia Civil barracks and workshop-school.

name: Palacio de Velarde
summary: The finest example of Renaissance architecture in the town, built in the mid-16th century for Alonso de Velarde and also known as the Palacio de las Arenas. Its most important restoration was carried out in 1934. The visit tells the story of Santillana and of the palace itself through holograms of the people who lived there and of its decorative features. Dogs are allowed.

name: Palacio de Peredo-Barreda
summary: One of the town's most elegant and singular buildings, the ensemble comprises the palace, its annexed houses and their splendid garden. It stands on an older Gothic tower or house of the Barreda family and was built around 1700 by Francisco Miguel de Peredo, whose lineage also owned the palaces of Mijares and Viveda. It is also called the Palacio de los Benemejís, as descendants of the Marchioness of Benemejís owned it until Caja Cantabria bought it. A modern cultural centre in the adjoining Velarde and Quijano houses runs a regular exhibition programme, and the restored palace, with its library and decorative and fine arts collections, is a new cultural space.

name: Palacio de Peredo-Barreda

name: Palacio de Sobrellano y Capilla Panteón
summary: Joan Martorell designed the Palacio de Sobrellano and its Chapel-Pantheon for the first Marquis of Comillas, Antonio López López, as a summer residence for the Marquis and the royal family: a neo-Gothic jewel with a Modernista aesthetic. The palace, begun in 1882 after the chapel, opened years after the second Marquis died. Octagonal, it has a central hall, a monumental stone staircase and a great salon with eight panels painted by Llorens. The chapel, a cathedral in miniature, has the pantheon below, a seat, prie-dieux and benches by Gaudí, paintings by Llorens and Masdeu, sculpture by Joan Roig and marble tombs by Llimona and Vallmitjana. BIC since 1981. The Chapel-Pantheon is closed for restoration.

name: Playa de Santa Justa (La Casa Azul)
summary: In the village of Ubiarco, the highlight is the Ermita de Santa Justa, a hermitage partly carved into the cliff rock, declared a Site of Local Interest in 2010. The present building dates from the 16th century and was consecrated thanks to relics of Saints Justa and Rufina; over time it became a pilgrimage centre for the region, one of the first on the Cantabrian coast. The remains of the Torre de San Telmo rise on the cliff above.

name: Puerto de Comillas (El Muelle)
summary: Comillas men seem to have taken up fishing on a significant scale only in the 16th century, because San Vicente de la Barquera held the exclusive right to fish the coast for two leagues east and west of its harbour. The oldest known ordinances of the Comillas fishermen's guild, the Cofradía de Pescadores del Santo Cristo del Amparo, date from 1522 and were revised in 1611. In the 17th century Comillas became the whaling capital of the Cantabrian Sea, and this wealth paid for its picturesque quays, its splendid parish church and its town hall.

name: Ría de San Martín de la Arena

name: Seminario Mayor de Comillas
summary: After the first Marquis died on 17 January 1883, his son Claudio López Bru had the plans drawn up, and the first stone was laid on 20 May 1883. The design was by Catalan architect Joan Martorell i Montells, who worked for the marquis in Barcelona and on the Sobrellano complex in Comillas. The Seminary belongs to late-19th-century Historicism, using Gothic and Mudéjar styles, then considered the true Spanish architecture. The visit can be combined with the Palacio and Chapel-Pantheon of Sobrellano; if buying online, leave at least 90–120 minutes between the two start times. Private parking costs €2, with €1 off for Seminary visitors.

name: Torre de Don Borja
summary: A 15th-century Gothic tower-house: two blocks joined by an unusual 16th-century courtyard. Declared a Site of Cultural Interest in 1943 with the whole town, it is named after Borja Barreda, holder of the entailed estate in 1844, and was also called Torre de don Borja-Bracho, La Torrona and Torre de la Infanta, after its owner Infanta Paz de Borbón. Ruined by the late 1970s, it was bought by Jesús Polanco and Pancho Pérez González for the Fundación Santillana; Luis Castillo's restoration won a Europa Nostra award, and he restored it again in 2019. It now holds a major private collection of contemporary Spanish art, a large Ibero-American library and the Infanta's historic library.
facts: Guided visits only (about 1 hour), by advance booking (several days ahead) by phone or email. No entry for under-12s for safety reasons; the building is not adapted for people with reduced mobility.

name: Torre de los Velarde
summary: A Gothic tower built in the mid-15th century by García de Velarde, head of one of the town's great lineages. It was substantially remodelled in the early 17th century.
facts: C/ Carrera, 5, Santillana del Mar, Cantabria

name: Torre del Merino
summary: A medieval Gothic tower of military character, built in the 14th century. It was the residence of the merino, the king's representative, after Santillana was made capital of the Asturias de Santillana in 1209, the largest jurisdiction in medieval Cantabria.

name: Universidad Pontificia
summary: An impressive neo-Gothic–Mudéjar building with Modernista decorative touches. Architect Miguel Alcoado led the first phase, and from 1884 the great Catalan architect Joan Martorell i Montells took over, with Cascante directing the works. Other leading masters collaborated too, among them Domènech i Montaner, who made the entrance portico and other ornamental features. Declared a Site of Cultural Interest (BIC) in 1985. The visit is to the Seminario Mayor (see that entry). Private parking costs €2, with €1 off for Seminary visitors.

name: Zoo de Santillana
summary: Covering 60,000 m², this private zoo has been rated by ADENA/WWF one of the four best zoos in Spain. It focuses on four main attractions: primates, big cats, tropical butterflies and waterfowl. Its 30,000 m² Parque Cuaternario themed area takes visitors back 14,000 years to when Altamira's people roamed these lands, with European bison, reindeer, Iberian wolves, roe deer, bears, deer, Przewalski's horses, European otters, capercaillie and a wide collection of northern waterfowl.
